igcse-0580-sequences-patterns.description: Count the fixed and repeated parts of diagrams, follow a term-to-term rule and compare two patterns.

sections.title: How do I count the part that grows?
sections.label: Count the parts

blocks.html: A drawing can change in one place and stay the same somewhere else. Count those two parts separately.

figure.alt: Stages 1, 2 and 3 use one, two and three panels respectively. Each panel has three lights. Each stage has two gold end lights.
figure.caption: The end lights stay fixed, while each new stage adds another three-light panel.

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html: In the lights diagram each stage adds one panel containing three lights. The two end lights stay in every stage. The first three totals are 5, 8 and 11.

blocks.title: Count the fixed and repeated parts of a pattern
blocks.prompt: A row of signs has 10 end lights altogether. At stage \(n\) it also has 4 lights in each of \(n\) repeated panels. The first three totals are \(14,\;18,\;22\). How many lights are there at stage 15?
blocks.solution:
The panels give \(4n\) lights at stage \(n\). The end lights do not change.

Use \(4n+10\). For stage 15, the total is \(70\).
blocks.hint: Separate the lights that are always present from the lights in the repeated panels.

retry.feedback: The panels are correct. Add the fixed end lights once.
Only the panels repeat. The end lights from stage one should not be repeated.

blocks.html: The end lights appear once at every stage. They do not belong inside the part that repeats.

blocks.title: Use a relationship between two patterns
blocks.prompt: Two strips grow in stages. Strip A has \(17,\;22,\;27\) tiles at stages 1 to 3 and grows by 5 tiles each stage. At the same stage, strip B has twice as many tiles as A, plus 5. Find the number of tiles in strip B at stage 4.
blocks.solution:
Strip A has \(32\) tiles at stage 4.

Double that stage's value and add 5. Strip B has \(69\) tiles.
blocks.hint: Compare the two strips at stage 4. Find A's value for that stage first.

retry.feedback: That uses A's stage-3 value. Extend strip A to stage 4 first.
Double the value and include the extra tiles.

sections.title: What operation takes me to the next term?
sections.label: Move one place

blocks.html: A term-to-term rule tells you what to do to one value to get the next. It needs a starting value before you can use it.

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html: For a constant-step pattern, subtract the earlier term from the later one. Keep the sign. For alternating rules, identify which of the two actions comes next.

blocks.title: Continue a constant-step sequence
blocks.prompt: These terms have a constant difference. Write the next term in \(19,\;14,\;9,\;4\).
blocks.solution:
Subtract one term from the term that follows it. Each change is \(-5\).

Add that signed change to \(4\) to get \(-1\).
blocks.hint: Find the change by subtracting the earlier term from the later term.

retry.feedback: When the sequence decreases, the step is negative.

blocks.html: Subtracting in reverse order changes the sign. An increasing sequence has a positive difference and a decreasing one has a negative difference.

blocks.title: Continue an alternating rule
blocks.prompt: The sequence starts \(33,\;41,\;37,\;45\). The rule alternates between adding 8 and subtracting 4, beginning with addition. Write the next term.
blocks.solution:
The last step shown adds 8. The next step subtracts 4.

The next term is \(45-4=41\).
blocks.hint: Look at the action between the last two terms, then swap to the other action.

retry.feedback: Addition has just been used. The next action is subtraction.
Use subtraction for the next step.

sections.title: What if the gaps change or I need two terms?
sections.label: Track changing gaps

blocks.html: Some patterns have their own rule for the gaps. For other patterns, add the two terms immediately before the gap.

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html: If the gaps increase by the same amount, extend the row of gaps first. If the rule says to add the two previous terms, use their values directly.

blocks.title: Continue a pattern of changing gaps
blocks.prompt: The sequence starts \(18,\;26,\;36,\;48\). Its positive gaps form a linear sequence. Find the next term.
blocks.solution:
The first three gaps are \(8,\;10,\;12\). They go up by 2 each time, so the next gap is 14.

Add it to the last term, \(48\), to get \(62\).
blocks.hint: Write the row of gaps before trying to find the next term.

retry.feedback: That is the next gap. Add it to the last term to find the next value.
The gaps increase. Extend the gap sequence by one place first.

blocks.html: A new gap is a change, not the next term. Add it to the last term to reach the next one.

blocks.title: Use the two preceding terms
blocks.prompt: The sequence begins \(12,\;7,\;19,\;26,\;45\). Each term after the second is the sum of the preceding two. Find the next term.
blocks.solution:
Use the final two terms shown, \(26\) and \(45\).

Their sum is \(71\).
blocks.hint: The rule uses two terms each time. Use the two immediately before the gap.

retry.feedback: Use the last term and the one before it.
Only the two immediately preceding terms count.

sections.title: How can I compare two patterns?
sections.label: Compare at the same stage

blocks.html: Place the position numbers above the terms before you compare. A relationship between two patterns usually refers to matching positions.

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html: If pattern B has twice as many pieces as A plus three more, find A at the required stage first. Double its count and add three.

blocks.title: Use a relationship between two patterns
blocks.prompt: Two strips grow in stages. Strip A has \(27,\;34,\;41\) tiles at stages 1 to 3 and grows by 7 tiles each stage. At the same stage, strip B has twice as many tiles as A, plus 10. Find the number of tiles in strip B at stage 4.
blocks.solution:
Strip A has \(48\) tiles at stage 4.

Double that stage's value and add 10. Strip B has \(106\) tiles.
blocks.hint: Compare the two strips at stage 4. Find A's value for that stage first.

retry.feedback: That uses A's stage-3 value. Extend strip A to stage 4 first.
Double the value and include the extra tiles.

revision.body:
How do I count the part that grows?

A drawing can change in one place and stay the same somewhere else. Count those two parts separately.

In the lights diagram each stage adds one panel containing three lights. The two end lights stay in every stage. The first three totals are 5, 8 and 11.

What operation takes me to the next term?

A term-to-term rule tells you what to do to one value to get the next. It needs a starting value before you can use it.

For a constant-step pattern, subtract the earlier term from the later one. Keep the sign. For alternating rules, identify which of the two actions comes next.

What if the gaps change or I need two terms?

Some patterns have their own rule for the gaps. For other patterns, add the two terms immediately before the gap.

If the gaps increase by the same amount, extend the row of gaps first. If the rule says to add the two previous terms, use their values directly.

How can I compare two patterns?

Place the position numbers above the terms before you compare. A relationship between two patterns usually refers to matching positions.

If pattern B has twice as many pieces as A plus three more, find A at the required stage first. Double its count and add three.

Quick worked example

A row of signs has 8 end lights altogether. At stage \(n\) it also has 2 lights in each of \(n\) repeated panels. The first three totals are \(10,\;12,\;14\). How many lights are there at stage 13?

The panels give \(2n\) lights at stage \(n\). The end lights do not change.

Use \(2n+8\). For stage 13, the total is \(34\).

  • Use the correct starting position.

sections.title: How can I write one rule for every position?
sections.label: Build the rule

blocks.html: A linear sequence has a constant difference \(d\). Its position-to-term formula has the form \(dn+c\).

figure.alt: Find the common step. Check position 1. Write the rule.
figure.caption: The step fixes the coefficient. The first term fixes the constant.

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html:
Find the common difference first. At position 1, \(dn\) already gives \(d\). Use the gap between that value and the actual first term to find \(c\).

blocks.title: Find the rule for any position
blocks.prompt: Find the \(n\)-th term of the linear sequence \(15,\;18,\;21,\;24\). Give an expression in \(n\).
blocks.solution:
The difference is \(3\). Start with \(3n\).

When \(n=1\), the formula must give \(15\). The adjustment is \(12\), so the rule is \(3n+12\).
blocks.hint: The common difference gives the coefficient of the position. Check the expression at position 1.

retry.feedback: The first term is the value when n = 1. The constant is the amount needed after the n-term has already contributed.

blocks.html: The adjustment \(c\) need not equal the first term. The expression must give the first term when \(n=1\).

blocks.title: Use a formula to jump to a later position
blocks.prompt: Sequence \(A\) has \(A_n=-5n+14\). Find \(A_{21}\).
blocks.solution:
The subscript tells you which position to use. Substitute \(n=21\).

The result is \(-91\).
blocks.hint: The subscript is the position, not a multiplier for the whole formula.

retry.feedback: The first term uses n = 1. Substitute the stated position directly.
Include the constant adjustment in the formula.

sections.title: How do I find a term far down the sequence?
sections.label: Substitute the position

blocks.html: The subscript in \(T_n\) labels the position. It tells you which number to substitute.

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html: Use the nth-term rule directly. For example, if \(T_n=37-4n\), substitute \(n=9\) to give \(T_9=1\).

blocks.title: Use a formula to jump to a later position
blocks.prompt: Sequence \(A\) has \(A_n=7n-25\). Find \(A_{17}\).
blocks.solution:
The subscript tells you which position to use. Substitute \(n=17\).

The result is \(94\).
blocks.hint: The subscript is the position, not a multiplier for the whole formula.

retry.feedback: The first term uses n = 1. Substitute the stated position directly.
Include the constant adjustment in the formula.

blocks.html: A decreasing sequence can go through zero into negative terms. Its position numbers are still positive integers.

blocks.title: Find the position of a given term
blocks.prompt: A sequence has \(T_n=9n+4\). At which position does the term \(148\) occur?
blocks.solution:
Set the term formula equal to \(148\). Solve \(9n+4=148\).

After removing the constant, divide by the common difference to get \(n=16\).
blocks.hint: This time the value is known. Use it as the other side of an equation for n.

retry.feedback: That is the term value. The question asks for the position in the sequence.
Positions start at 1. Your answer is one step too early.

sections.title: How can I tell whether a value occurs?
sections.label: Solve for the position

blocks.html: Set the formula equal to the stated value and solve for the position. A valid position is a positive whole number.

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html: If solving gives a fractional or non-positive position, explain what this means for the sequence. Substitute a possible position back into the rule to check it.

blocks.title: Find the position of a given term
blocks.prompt: A sequence has \(T_n=-2n+15\). At which position does the term \(-9\) occur?
blocks.solution:
Set the term formula equal to \(-9\). Solve \(-2n+15=-9\).

After removing the constant, divide by the common difference to get \(n=12\).
blocks.hint: This time the value is known. Use it as the other side of an equation for n.

retry.feedback: That is the term value. The question asks for the position in the sequence.
Positions start at 1. Your answer is one step too early.

blocks.html: Rounding a fractional position changes the term value. State that the target does not occur.

A nonconstant sequence made by repeatedly multiplying by a fixed non-zero factor.

revision.body:
What operation gives the same multiplier?

An exponential sequence multiplies each term by the same factor. Divide one term by the previous one to find the common ratio.

Compare at least two ratios. Equal differences suggest a linear rule. Equal non-zero ratios in a nonconstant sequence suggest repeated multiplication.

Why does the exponent start at zero?

There are no steps before the first term. With first term \(a\) and ratio \(r\), write \(T_n=ar^{n-1}\).

Substitute \(n=1\) to check that the factor is \(r^0=1\). Substitute \(n=2\) to check that the multiplier is used once.

How do I find where a power occurs?

Divide the target term by the starting term. Find how many repeated factors the result contains.

The exponent gives the number of steps from position 1. Add one to reach the position number. For the small integer powers here, a list of powers is enough.

Can the repeated multiplier make the terms smaller?

A positive multiplier below 1 makes positive terms smaller. Halving uses the multiplier \(\frac12\).

In \(a(\frac12)^{n-1}\), substitute the position before evaluating the power. Multiplying by one half is the same as dividing by two.

Quick worked example

The terms \(15,\;60,\;\square,\;960,\;3840\) are consecutive in an exponential sequence. Find the missing term.

The first two values give the multiplier \(4\). Apply it once to \(60\).

The missing value is \(240\). Multiplying this by \(4\) gives the fourth term.

revision.body:
Which values do I combine?

If \(C_n=A_n-2B_n\), use the same position \(n\) in both component sequences. Then take twice the B term away from the A term.

Work out the two values first when asked for one position. For a polynomial expression, substitute the two formulas and collect like terms.

What does a change of subscript do?

The rule \(B_n=A_{n+2}\) uses a later term of A. Position 1 of B takes position 3 of A.

Work out the new position before using the first sequence's formula. Write both positions explicitly so you can keep track of them.

How do I find a rule for a sequence of fractions?

Read all the given numerators as one sequence and all the denominators as another. Use the fractions as displayed so that you can see both patterns.

Find a rule for each row at the same position, then put the numerator rule over the denominator rule. Use brackets around any whole expression you type into an answer field.

Quick worked example

Let \(A_n=16\times 5^{n-1}\) and \(B_n=5n+14\). If \(C_n=A_n-2B_n\), find \(C_{9}\).

At position 9, the values are \(A_{9}=6250000\) and \(B_{9}=59\).

Subtract twice the value of B from the value of A. This gives \(6249882\).
